scenario: A bank has a labeled dataset of past loan applications with a column indicating whether each applicant defaulted. The bank wants to train an ML model to predict defaults for new applicants. Which type of machine learning is most appropriate?
correct_explanation: Supervised learning trains a model on labeled examples — input features paired with a known target (defaulted: yes/no). The trained model can then predict the target for new, unlabeled examples. The presence of historical labels is the defining signal.
wrong_explanation_1: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction). It does not predict a known target like default vs no-default.
wrong_explanation_2: Reinforcement learning trains agents through rewards from interacting with an environment. There is no interactive environment in a default-prediction task.
wrong_explanation_3: Self-supervised pre-training generates pseudo-labels from the data itself for tasks like LLM training. It is not the standard approach for tabular classification with explicit labels.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL)?
correct_answer: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
wrong_answer_1: Artificial intelligence is a subset of deep learning
wrong_answer_2: Machine learning and deep learning are unrelated fields
wrong_answer_3: Deep learning and artificial intelligence are the same field, with machine learning as a separate discipline
correct_explanation: AI is the broadest field — systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence. ML is a subset of AI in which systems learn from data. DL is a subset of ML using deep neural networks with many layers. The nesting is DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI.
wrong_explanation_1: The hierarchy is reversed — AI is the broader field that contains ML and DL.
wrong_explanation_2: ML and DL are related; DL is a specific kind of ML.
wrong_explanation_3: DL is not equivalent to AI. AI is broader and predates deep learning.

scenario: A robotics team trains a robotic arm to stack blocks. The arm receives positive numerical feedback when it stacks correctly and negative feedback when it knocks blocks over, learning over many trials. Which type of ML does this describe?
correct_explanation: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through trial-and-error interactions with an environment, with a reward signal indicating better or worse outcomes. The block-stacking scenario fits exactly: actions, environment, and a reward signal.
wrong_explanation_1: Supervised learning requires labeled examples of correct stacks; the scenario describes an agent learning by trying actions and observing rewards.
wrong_explanation_2: Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data. It is not an agent-and-reward paradigm.
wrong_explanation_3: Anomaly detection identifies outliers, not stacking behavior learned from rewards.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes what an embedding is in the context of machine learning?
correct_answer: A dense vector representation of text, image, or other input that captures semantic meaning in a fixed-dimensional space
wrong_answer_1: A web page that displays a model's training metrics
wrong_answer_2: A type of hyperparameter that controls learning rate
wrong_answer_3: A configuration file that defines a Lambda function
correct_explanation: Embeddings are numerical vector representations of data — text, images, or audio — placed in a continuous space so semantically similar items are close together. They are foundational to modern search, recommendation, and LLM workflows.
wrong_explanation_1: An embeddings dashboard is not the embedding itself; the embedding is the underlying vector representation.
wrong_explanation_2: A learning-rate hyperparameter controls optimization. It is unrelated to vector representations of data.
wrong_explanation_3: A Lambda configuration is unrelated to ML embeddings.

scenario: A retailer keeps three datasets: (a) a CSV file of weekly sales totals, (b) a JSON file with nested product attributes, and (c) a folder of customer support call recordings. Which describes these datasets MOST accurately?
correct_answer: Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, respectively
correct_explanation: A CSV of fixed columns is structured (tabular). A JSON file has tags and nesting but no strict tabular schema — semi-structured. Audio recordings have no inherent schema and require ML to extract meaning — unstructured.
wrong_explanation_1: The categories are mapped in the wrong order. CSVs are structured, not unstructured.
wrong_explanation_2: JSON and audio do not fit the strict tabular form of structured data.
wrong_explanation_3: A CSV with year, week, and total columns is structured tabular data.

scenario: A publisher wants to automatically convert printed books into natural-sounding spoken audio in several voices and languages. Which AWS service is the BEST fit for the text-to-speech step?
correct_explanation: Amazon Polly converts text to lifelike speech in multiple voices and languages. It is the AWS managed service purpose-built for text-to-speech, the exact step in the scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: Transcribe converts speech to text — the opposite direction.
wrong_explanation_2: Translate converts text between languages but does not produce audio.
wrong_explanation_3: Lex builds conversational chatbots; it is not a dedicated text-to-speech service.

scenario: A claims processing team needs to automatically extract printed text, handwriting, and form fields (key-value pairs) from scanned PDF documents. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Textract is the AWS service for extracting text, handwriting, key-value pairs, and tables from scanned documents and PDFs. It returns structured output suited to downstream automation.
wrong_explanation_1: Rekognition analyzes images and videos for objects, faces, and moderation. It is not built for extracting form fields and tables from documents.
wrong_explanation_2: Comprehend performs NLP (entity recognition, sentiment, key phrases) on text but does not extract text from images of documents.
wrong_explanation_3: Transcribe converts spoken audio to text; it is not a document-OCR service.

scenario: A photo-sharing application needs to detect objects, scenes, and inappropriate content in user uploads, plus identify faces. Which AWS managed AI service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Rekognition uses pre-trained ML models for image and video analysis — object/scene detection, content moderation, face analysis, and celebrity recognition. It is the AWS managed service for these computer-vision tasks.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Canvas is a no-code ML builder for custom models on tabular data, not a vision API.
wrong_explanation_2: Textract extracts text and forms from documents — not general image analysis.
wrong_explanation_3: Comprehend works on text, not images.

scenario: An online retailer wants to provide personalized product recommendations for each shopper based on their browsing and purchase history, without building a custom recommendation algorithm from scratch. Which AWS service is the BEST fit?
correct_explanation: Amazon Personalize is the AWS managed service for personalized recommendation systems. It uses customer interaction data, user features, and item features to produce real-time recommendations without custom algorithm work.
wrong_explanation_1: Forecast is for time-series forecasting (e.g., demand or revenue prediction), not personalized recommendations.
wrong_explanation_2: Kendra is an intelligent enterprise search service; it is not built for personalized product recommendation.
wrong_explanation_3: Comprehend is for NLP — entity recognition, sentiment, and key phrases — not for recommendations.

scenario: In the standard ML development lifecycle, which phase involves collecting raw data, handling missing values, removing outliers, and engineering features?
correct_explanation: Data preparation (also called preprocessing) is the lifecycle phase covering collection, cleaning, handling missing values, removing outliers, and engineering features. Quality of this phase directly determines model performance.
wrong_explanation_1: Deployment moves a trained model into production; it does not handle raw data preparation.
wrong_explanation_2: Monitoring observes model behavior after deployment.
wrong_explanation_3: Business problem framing defines the goal and success criteria but does not perform data cleaning.

scenario: Why does a typical ML workflow split data into separate training, validation, and test sets?
correct_answer: To tune hyperparameters on the validation set while keeping the test set untouched for an unbiased final performance estimate
wrong_answer_1: To speed up training by processing the three sets in parallel
wrong_answer_2: To enable ensemble methods that train different models on each subset
wrong_answer_3: To apply different preprocessing techniques to each subset
correct_explanation: The training set fits the model, the validation set tunes hyperparameters and informs model selection, and the test set provides an unbiased final estimate of generalization. Keeping the test set untouched until the end prevents leakage.
wrong_explanation_1: Parallelism is unrelated to the purpose of the split.
wrong_explanation_2: Ensembles do not require this three-way split.
wrong_explanation_3: Preprocessing decisions should be consistent across splits to avoid leakage; they are not the reason for the split.

scenario: A data scientist needs to tune the learning rate and regularization strength of a model, evaluating many combinations to find the configuration that performs best on a held-out dataset. Which activity does this describe?
correct_explanation: Hyperparameter tuning is the process of searching across hyperparameter values (learning rate, regularization, etc.) and choosing the configuration that performs best on validation data. SageMaker offers Automatic Model Tuning for this.
wrong_explanation_1: Feature engineering creates and transforms input features. It is not about searching hyperparameters.
wrong_explanation_2: Deployment places a trained model in production; it does not involve a sweep of hyperparameters.
wrong_explanation_3: Labeling assigns ground-truth tags to data; it is unrelated to hyperparameter search.

scenario: A company has deployed a model to production. The team wants to detect changes in the statistical properties of incoming inference data versus the training distribution. Which capability addresses this need?
correct_answer: Model and data drift monitoring (Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor)
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor continuously monitors deployed endpoints for data quality and model quality drift, including statistical comparison of inference data against a baseline taken during training. Drift detection is exactly the capability described.
wrong_explanation_1: Ground Truth is a labeling service for training datasets, not a production drift monitor.
wrong_explanation_2: JumpStart is a hub of pre-trained models and solutions, not a drift monitor.
wrong_explanation_3: Studio notebooks are development environments, not production monitoring services.

scenario: Which statement BEST describes a foundation model (FM)?
correct_answer: A large, general-purpose model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
wrong_answer_1: A small model trained for a single, specific task and not useful elsewhere
wrong_answer_2: A rule-based system written by hand that does not use neural networks
wrong_answer_3: A type of relational database optimized for time-series queries
correct_explanation: Foundation models are large models pre-trained on broad, diverse data (text, code, images). They develop general capabilities that can be adapted (via prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning) to many downstream tasks rather than being trained per-task from scratch.
wrong_explanation_1: FMs are explicitly general-purpose and reusable, the opposite of single-task narrow models.
wrong_explanation_2: FMs are neural-network-based models, not hand-coded rule systems.
wrong_explanation_3: FMs are not databases.

scenario: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of a large language model (LLM)?
correct_answer: A neural network with a very large number of parameters trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text
wrong_answer_1: A linear regression model fit on text data
wrong_answer_2: A database engine optimized for storing language documents
wrong_answer_3: A rule-based system that performs grammar correction only
correct_explanation: LLMs are large transformer-based neural networks with billions of parameters trained — at scale — to predict the next token (and related self-supervised objectives) over enormous text corpora. This is what gives them their general language abilities.
wrong_explanation_1: Linear regression cannot model language at the scale and complexity LLMs do.
wrong_explanation_2: LLMs are not databases.
wrong_explanation_3: Rule-based grammar tools are narrow, hand-engineered systems — not LLMs.

scenario: In the context of large language models, what does the term "token" refer to?
correct_answer: A unit of text (often a word piece) that the model processes as input or output
wrong_answer_1: An authentication credential used to call the model's API
wrong_answer_2: A row in a training database
wrong_answer_3: A type of GPU memory cache
correct_explanation: Tokens are the discrete units (subword pieces, words, or characters) that LLMs ingest and emit. Pricing, context windows, and response length limits are commonly measured in tokens.
wrong_explanation_1: API access tokens for authentication share a name but are unrelated to model tokenization.
wrong_explanation_2: Training data rows are not tokens.
wrong_explanation_3: GPU memory caches are hardware concepts, not text units.

scenario: A marketing team wants to generate original images from natural-language descriptions like "a watercolor painting of a mountain at sunset". Which type of generative model is BEST suited for this task?
correct_explanation: Diffusion models are the dominant architecture behind modern text-to-image generation. They iteratively refine random noise into coherent images conditioned on a text prompt, producing original images from descriptions.
wrong_explanation_1: Linear regression predicts continuous targets; it cannot synthesize novel images.
wrong_explanation_2: Decision trees split data on feature thresholds; they are not image generators.
wrong_explanation_3: k-NN finds similar examples and cannot generate new images from text.

scenario: A team is evaluating a foundation model that can accept both text and images as input and produce text descriptions. Which term BEST describes this kind of model?
correct_explanation: Multimodal models handle more than one modality of data (e.g., text + image + audio) and can map across modalities — for example, taking an image as input and producing a text caption. Modern foundation models increasingly support multimodal input.
wrong_explanation_1: Linear models do not span multiple modalities like images and text.
wrong_explanation_2: RNNs are a single architecture family; multimodality is defined by input/output type, not architecture.
wrong_explanation_3: CNNs alone are not enough to caption images with natural language descriptions — multimodal foundation models combine vision and language capability.

scenario: A team notices that their LLM confidently generates factual-sounding statements that are actually incorrect — citing fake papers or attributing quotes to people who never said them. What is this phenomenon commonly called?
correct_explanation: Hallucination is the term for an LLM producing confident, fluent output that is factually wrong or fabricated. Hallucinations are a fundamental limitation of generative LLMs and are often mitigated with RAG, guardrails, or constrained decoding.
wrong_explanation_1: Drift refers to changes in data or model behavior over time, not to fabricated factual content.
wrong_explanation_2: Overfitting is an ML training problem where a model memorizes training data; it differs from confidently fabricated content during inference.
wrong_explanation_3: Quantization reduces numerical precision of a model's weights to save memory; it is unrelated.

scenario: A company wants to choose between using a small, less capable foundation model and a large, more capable one. Which trade-off is MOST relevant when making this decision?
correct_answer: Higher capability models typically cost more per token and have higher latency than smaller models
wrong_answer_1: Larger foundation models are always free, while smaller ones are paid
wrong_answer_2: Smaller models always outperform larger models on every task
wrong_answer_3: Model size has no impact on cost or latency
correct_explanation: Larger FMs are more capable but typically incur higher cost per token and higher inference latency than smaller models. Teams must weigh the quality-versus-cost-and-latency trade-off based on the task requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Larger FMs are not free; they typically cost more per token, not less.
wrong_explanation_2: Smaller models can win on cost or speed and are sometimes good enough, but they do not categorically outperform larger ones.
wrong_explanation_3: Model size has substantial effects on both cost and latency.

scenario: A research analyst needs an LLM to summarize a 200-page report in a single prompt-response interaction. Which foundation-model property MUST be large enough to accept this input?
correct_explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single request (prompt + response). To pass a 200-page document in one call, the FM's context window must accommodate the entire input plus space for the output.
wrong_explanation_1: Top-K controls token-sampling diversity; it has nothing to do with input length capacity.
wrong_explanation_2: Temperature controls randomness, not input size.
wrong_explanation_3: Stop sequences truncate output at specific tokens; they do not expand input capacity.

scenario: A company is using a foundation model for HR resume screening. The team notices the model recommends candidates from certain demographic groups more often, even when qualifications are similar. Which limitation of generative AI is at play?
correct_explanation: Foundation models can reflect and amplify biases present in their training data. Deployed in high-stakes processes like hiring, this bias can produce disparate impact across demographic groups. Mitigating bias and applying responsible AI controls is essential.
wrong_explanation_1: Hallucination is about generating false content; the scenario is about systematic preference for groups.
wrong_explanation_2: Latency is about response time, not group-level outcome disparity.
wrong_explanation_3: Context window size affects how much input the model can process, not group-level bias.

scenario: A startup wants to evaluate whether generative AI is suitable for a task before investing in a full implementation. Which factor argues AGAINST using a foundation model when accuracy and reproducibility are paramount?
correct_answer: Generative AI outputs can be probabilistic and non-deterministic, varying between identical requests
wrong_answer_1: Generative AI models cannot accept user input
wrong_answer_2: Generative AI cannot produce text in English
wrong_answer_3: Generative AI requires zero compute resources
correct_explanation: By design, generative LLMs produce probabilistic outputs that can vary between identical requests (especially at non-zero temperature). For workflows requiring strict reproducibility or numerical precision, this variability is a limitation to account for.
wrong_explanation_1: Generative AI explicitly responds to user input.
wrong_explanation_2: Generative AI commonly produces text in many languages including English.
wrong_explanation_3: Generative AI is compute-intensive at inference and training.

scenario: A company wants a single AWS managed service to access multiple high-quality foundation models from different providers (such as Anthropic Claude, Amazon Titan, Meta Llama, AI21, and Cohere) through one API. Which service should they use?
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock is the AWS managed service for accessing foundation models from multiple top providers via a single API. It supports models from Anthropic, Amazon (Titan and Nova), Meta, Cohere, AI21, and others — without managing infrastructure.
wrong_explanation_1: SageMaker Canvas is a no-code ML builder for tabular ML, not a multi-provider FM API.
wrong_explanation_2: Polly is a text-to-speech service, not a foundation-model gateway.
wrong_explanation_3: DeepLens (now discontinued) was a deep-learning enabled camera for developers, not an FM gateway.

scenario: A data scientist wants to discover, browse, and quickly deploy pre-trained models and prebuilt ML solutions across many task types — including foundation models — from a curated hub inside Amazon SageMaker. Which feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: SageMaker JumpStart is a model and solution hub curated by AWS. It includes built-in algorithms, prebuilt solutions, and foundation models with one-click deployment options inside SageMaker.
wrong_explanation_1: Model Monitor watches deployed endpoints for drift, not a model hub.
wrong_explanation_2: Ground Truth is a data-labeling service.
wrong_explanation_3: Pipelines orchestrate ML workflows, not model browsing and deployment.

scenario: A business team without coding skills wants to experiment with generative AI by chaining prompts and building small AI "mini-apps" in a browser, powered by foundation models on AWS. Which AWS offering is purpose-built for this no-code generative-AI experimentation?
correct_explanation: PartyRock is an Amazon Bedrock-powered playground that lets users create small generative-AI applications in a browser by composing prompts and widgets without writing code — built for hands-on experimentation.
wrong_explanation_1: Studio Lab is a free environment for running Jupyter notebooks; it is code-based, not no-code app building.
wrong_explanation_2: DeepRacer teaches reinforcement learning with autonomous race cars — unrelated to no-code gen-AI mini-apps.
wrong_explanation_3: Cloud9 is a developer IDE, not a no-code gen-AI playground.

scenario: An enterprise wants a generative AI assistant that employees can chat with to ask questions and summarize internal company documents stored in S3, Confluence, and SharePoint, with permissions respected per user. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Q Business is a managed generative AI assistant tailored for enterprise data. It connects to many enterprise sources (S3, SharePoint, Confluence, etc.), respects per-user permissions, and answers and summarizes using a foundation model.
wrong_explanation_1: Amazon Q Developer is the AI coding companion for software engineers — different audience and capability than enterprise document chat.
wrong_explanation_2: Lex builds intent-based chatbots and IVR flows; it is not a managed enterprise-data Q&A assistant.
wrong_explanation_3: Kendra is an enterprise search engine and is often a building block for retrieval, but Q Business is the end-to-end managed assistant the scenario describes.

scenario: A development team wants an AI coding companion that generates code suggestions, explains code, and helps fix issues inside their IDE. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this developer experience?
correct_explanation: Amazon Q Developer is the AI coding companion in the IDE and console. It suggests code, helps debug, explains code, and accelerates AWS-related development tasks.
wrong_explanation_1: Q Business targets knowledge-worker / enterprise data Q&A, not in-IDE code generation.
wrong_explanation_2: Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks calling APIs and knowledge bases; they are not the IDE-integrated developer assistant.
wrong_explanation_3: Cloud9 alone is an IDE — it does not provide AI coding suggestions without an assistant like Q Developer.

scenario: A team wants purpose-built AWS hardware that accelerates the TRAINING of large foundation models with lower cost than GPU instances. Which AWS infrastructure offering should they choose?
correct_explanation: AWS Trainium is the AWS custom silicon optimized for deep-learning training. Trn1 (and newer) instances offer compelling price-performance for training large models compared with general-purpose GPUs.
wrong_explanation_1: AWS Inferentia is optimized for inference, not training. (Inf1/Inf2 are the inference instances; Trn1 is for training.)
wrong_explanation_2: Burstable T-class instances are general-purpose, not ML accelerators.
wrong_explanation_3: Snowcone is a rugged data transfer device with limited edge compute — not a training accelerator.

scenario: A team wants their generative AI assistant to answer questions using the company's internal product documentation rather than relying solely on the foundation model's pre-trained knowledge. Which pattern BEST meets this requirement?
correct_explanation: RAG augments an FM at inference time by retrieving relevant chunks of company-specific documents (typically from a vector store) and injecting them into the prompt. The FM then grounds its answer in that retrieved content rather than relying solely on its parametric knowledge.
wrong_explanation_1: RLHF refines a model with human feedback during training; it does not directly retrieve company documents at inference time.
wrong_explanation_2: Hyperparameter tuning optimizes training settings, not retrieval grounding.
wrong_explanation_3: Quantization reduces model size; it does not ground responses in company data.

scenario: A team wants to build a RAG application on AWS with the LEAST operational overhead — connecting an S3-hosted document set to a foundation model so user queries get grounded answers. Which Amazon Bedrock feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the managed RAG capability in Bedrock. Customers point it at an S3 source and a supported vector store, and Bedrock handles ingestion, embedding, retrieval, and augmentation — minimizing custom integration work.
wrong_explanation_1: Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks and tool/API calls. They use Knowledge Bases as one source but are not themselves the managed RAG capability.
wrong_explanation_2: Guardrails filter harmful content and apply policies; they are not the RAG retrieval mechanism.
wrong_explanation_3: Custom model imports bring fine-tuned models into Bedrock; that is unrelated to RAG retrieval.

scenario: A search team needs a managed AWS database that stores embedding vectors and supports approximate nearest neighbor (k-NN) similarity search to power semantic retrieval. Which AWS service is purpose-built for vector storage and search?
correct_answer: Amazon OpenSearch Service (with the k-NN plugin and vector engine)
wrong_answer_1: Amazon Aurora MySQL (with no vector extension)
correct_explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Service supports vector storage and approximate nearest neighbor search through the k-NN plugin and the OpenSearch vector engine, making it a primary AWS option for semantic retrieval. AWS also supports vector capability in services like Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and Amazon MemoryDB.
wrong_explanation_1: Plain Aurora MySQL without a vector extension does not natively support efficient similarity search over embeddings.
wrong_explanation_2: QuickSight is a BI service, not a vector database.
wrong_explanation_3: Athena queries data in place using SQL; it is not a managed vector database.

scenario: Which step BEST describes how text documents are typically prepared for retrieval in a RAG system?
correct_answer: Split documents into chunks, generate embedding vectors for each chunk, and store the vectors in a vector index keyed to their source chunk
wrong_answer_1: Convert every document into a single training example used to fine-tune the foundation model
wrong_answer_2: Encrypt the documents and store them in a relational database with no chunking
wrong_answer_3: Discard the documents after one use
correct_explanation: The standard RAG pipeline chunks long documents into smaller passages, embeds each chunk into a vector, and indexes those vectors in a vector store. At query time, the user query is embedded and similar chunks are retrieved and inserted into the FM's prompt.
wrong_explanation_1: Treating each document as a fine-tune example describes fine-tuning, not retrieval-time grounding.
wrong_explanation_2: Encryption is orthogonal to retrieval; storing raw docs in a relational DB without embeddings does not enable semantic similarity search.
wrong_explanation_3: Discarding documents removes the source of grounding entirely.

scenario: A team needs a generative AI assistant that can not only answer questions but also TAKE ACTIONS on behalf of users — calling internal APIs to look up orders, update tickets, and trigger workflows. Which Amazon Bedrock feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks by combining an FM's reasoning with action groups that call APIs and use knowledge bases. Agents are the right Bedrock primitive for assistants that must take real actions.
wrong_explanation_1: Knowledge Bases provide retrieval grounding; they do not by themselves invoke APIs and execute multi-step plans.
wrong_explanation_2: Guardrails filter harmful content and enforce policies; they do not invoke actions.
wrong_explanation_3: Custom models customize the underlying FM; they do not provide the agentic, tool-using workflow.

scenario: A user asks a foundation model to classify a sentence as positive or negative WITHOUT providing any example labeled sentences in the prompt. Which prompt engineering technique does this represent?
correct_explanation: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to perform a task with no in-prompt examples — relying on the model's pre-trained knowledge. The scenario matches exactly because no labeled examples are included.
wrong_explanation_1: Few-shot includes a few labeled examples before the user's question; the scenario explicitly excludes them.
wrong_explanation_2: Chain-of-thought asks the model to show its reasoning steps; it is not defined by example count.
wrong_explanation_3: ReAct combines reasoning and tool use; it is unrelated to whether examples are included.

scenario: A prompt for an LLM includes three labeled example inputs and outputs before posing the actual task, to help the model generalize the desired pattern. Which prompt engineering technique does this represent?
correct_explanation: Few-shot prompting provides a small number of input-output examples directly in the prompt. The examples help the model understand the desired pattern before performing the actual task.
wrong_explanation_1: Zero-shot prompting has no examples, the opposite of the scenario.
wrong_explanation_2: RAG retrieves external documents at inference time; it is not the same as including labeled examples inline.
wrong_explanation_3: Fine-tuning modifies the model's weights; it is not done at prompt time.

scenario: A team needs an LLM to solve a multi-step word problem and shows its intermediate reasoning steps in the response. Which prompt engineering technique BEST elicits this behavior?
correct_explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting instructs the model to explicitly show its intermediate reasoning steps before producing the final answer. This often improves accuracy on multi-step problems.
wrong_explanation_1: Plain zero-shot prompting does not by itself elicit step-by-step reasoning.
wrong_explanation_2: Negative prompting asks the model to avoid certain content; it is unrelated to multi-step reasoning.
wrong_explanation_3: Prompt compression shortens prompts; it does not elicit reasoning.

scenario: An LLM keeps producing slightly different outputs for the same prompt. The team wants more deterministic, focused responses. Which inference parameter change is MOST appropriate?
correct_explanation: Temperature controls the randomness of token sampling. Lowering temperature (closer to 0) makes the model favor the highest-probability tokens, producing more deterministic and focused outputs.
wrong_explanation_1: Higher temperature increases randomness — the opposite of what the team wants.
wrong_explanation_2: Higher Top-P widens the sampling pool, also increasing diversity.
wrong_explanation_3: Stop sequences end generation when matched; they do not control determinism.

scenario: An image-generation model keeps producing images that include text labels in them, but the team wants images WITHOUT any text labels overlaid. Which prompt engineering technique BEST addresses this with the least operational effort?
correct_answer: Use a negative prompt that lists "text" and "labels" as content to avoid
wrong_answer_1: Fine-tune the model on a custom dataset that has no text labels
wrong_answer_2: Train a brand-new diffusion model from scratch
wrong_answer_3: Lower the temperature parameter to zero
correct_explanation: Negative prompts let users specify content the model should avoid generating. Listing "text" and "labels" as negative-prompt entries is a low-effort, prompt-engineering-only way to suppress that content in image generation.
wrong_explanation_1: Fine-tuning is heavy operational work for what can be accomplished with a negative prompt.
wrong_explanation_2: Training a brand-new model is even heavier and unnecessary.
wrong_explanation_3: Temperature controls randomness; it does not specifically suppress "text" in image output.

scenario: A company has a labeled dataset of 5,000 product-support emails paired with the correct categorical tag. They want to customize a foundation model so it categorizes new emails accurately. Which model-customization technique is BEST suited?
correct_explanation: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model's weights using a labeled, task-specific dataset. A labeled set of email/category pairs is the canonical input for fine-tuning a classification-style task.
wrong_explanation_1: Continued pre-training uses UNLABELED domain data to further pre-train an FM. The scenario specifies labeled pairs, which suits fine-tuning.
wrong_explanation_2: RAG grounds responses in external documents at inference time; it does not adapt model weights for a categorization task.
wrong_explanation_3: Prompt engineering can help but doesn't shift model weights for the specific labeled categories the team has.

scenario: A company has a large corpus of UNLABELED domain-specific legal text and wants to further train a foundation model so it generally performs better in the legal domain — without targeting a specific labeled task. Which customization technique is BEST suited?
correct_explanation: Continued pre-training extends a foundation model's pre-training using a large unlabeled domain corpus. The result is a model that has internalized the domain's vocabulary, style, and knowledge — well-suited to general legal text without a specific labeled task.
wrong_explanation_1: Fine-tuning requires labeled examples for a specific task; this scenario explicitly says the data is unlabeled and no specific task is targeted.
wrong_explanation_2: RAG augments at inference time and does not adapt the underlying model.
wrong_explanation_3: Prompt engineering does not adapt the model itself for a specialized domain at scale.

scenario: A team has trained a model and wants to align its responses with human preferences — making them more helpful and less harmful — using human-provided rankings of model outputs. Which technique BEST describes this workflow?
correct_explanation: RLHF aligns model outputs with human preferences by using a reward model trained on human rankings, then optimizing the LLM using reinforcement learning against that reward. It is the canonical alignment technique behind many modern chat models.
wrong_explanation_1: Continued pre-training is unlabeled domain training, not preference alignment.
wrong_explanation_2: RAG augments responses with retrieved documents; it does not align preferences.
wrong_explanation_3: Few-shot prompting modifies prompts, not the model's underlying behavior.

scenario: Which model customization technique modifies the actual WEIGHTS of a foundation model rather than only changing prompts or retrieved context?
correct_explanation: Fine-tuning updates the model's parameters using a task-specific labeled dataset, modifying weights. Continued pre-training also changes weights. Prompting and RAG operate at inference time and do not change weights.
wrong_explanation_1: RAG only augments the prompt with retrieved documents; weights are unchanged.
wrong_explanation_2: Few-shot prompting modifies the prompt content; weights are unchanged.
wrong_explanation_3: Negative prompting also modifies the prompt; weights are unchanged.

scenario: A team is evaluating a foundation model used for TEXT SUMMARIZATION and wants to compare model-generated summaries against human-written reference summaries by measuring overlap of words and n-grams. Which metric is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a set of metrics designed to compare machine-generated summaries with reference summaries by measuring overlap (recall, precision, F1) of n-grams and longest common subsequences.
wrong_explanation_1: BLEU is designed primarily for machine translation evaluation, focusing on precision of n-grams.
wrong_explanation_2: RMSE is a regression metric for numerical predictions, not text summarization.
wrong_explanation_3: Accuracy is a classification metric; summaries are open-ended generation.

scenario: Which evaluation metric is most commonly associated with comparing MACHINE TRANSLATION output against human reference translations using n-gram precision?
correct_explanation: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) measures the n-gram precision of machine-generated translations against reference translations. It is the canonical translation-evaluation metric.
wrong_explanation_1: ROUGE focuses on summarization quality using recall-oriented overlap, not translation precision.
wrong_explanation_2: mAP is for object detection or ranked retrieval, not text translation evaluation.
wrong_explanation_3: Toxicity scores measure harmful content level, not translation quality.

scenario: An AI team wants to evaluate several foundation models on Amazon Bedrock using automatic metrics (accuracy, robustness, toxicity) and built-in or custom datasets. Which Amazon Bedrock feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs let users automatically or with human feedback evaluate one or more FMs on metrics like accuracy, robustness, and toxicity, using built-in or custom datasets. Reports highlight relative strengths to guide model selection.
wrong_explanation_1: Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks; they are not evaluation tools.
wrong_explanation_2: Knowledge Bases provide retrieval grounding for RAG; they do not evaluate model quality.
wrong_explanation_3: Guardrails enforce content policies but do not perform comparative model evaluation.

scenario: A team wants humans to grade the LINGUISTIC QUALITY of an LLM's open-ended marketing copy — including coherence and creativity — using consistent rubrics, then aggregate those judgments. Which evaluation approach is MOST appropriate?
correct_explanation: When evaluating open-ended subjective qualities like creativity and coherence, human judgment with structured rubrics is more reliable than automatic metrics. Bedrock model evaluation supports human-in-the-loop evaluation precisely for these qualities.
wrong_explanation_1: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap and does not capture creativity or coherence judgments.
wrong_explanation_2: BLEU is for machine translation precision; it is not suited to subjective marketing-copy quality.
wrong_explanation_3: Mean squared error is a regression metric for numerical predictions, not text quality.

scenario: A bank uses an ML model for credit decisions and discovers the model approves men at a meaningfully higher rate than equally qualified women. Which AWS service is purpose-built to help detect and explain this kind of bias?
correct_explanation: Amazon SageMaker Clarify detects bias in data and in trained models across protected attributes, and provides explainability (feature attributions) to help identify why a model is producing biased outcomes. It is the dedicated AWS bias-and-explainability service.
wrong_explanation_1: Model Monitor watches deployed endpoints for drift; it is not the dedicated bias-detection and explainability tool.
wrong_explanation_2: Pipelines orchestrate ML workflows; they do not detect bias.
wrong_explanation_3: Feature Store stores reusable features; it does not analyze bias.

scenario: Which responsible AI dimension involves considering whether a model produces equitable outcomes across different groups of users?
correct_explanation: Fairness is the responsible AI dimension concerned with whether an AI system's outcomes are equitable across groups, avoiding disparate impact and discrimination. It is one of AWS's core responsible AI dimensions.
wrong_explanation_1: Veracity and robustness focus on correctness even under adversarial or unexpected inputs.
wrong_explanation_2: Explainability concerns whether system outputs can be understood and justified.
wrong_explanation_3: Privacy concerns protection of personal data, not equitable outcomes.

scenario: A model is found to fail catastrophically when users provide slightly perturbed or adversarial inputs. Which responsible AI dimension is MOST directly concerned with this property?
correct_explanation: Veracity and robustness focus on producing correct, reliable outputs even with unexpected, noisy, or adversarial inputs. A model that breaks on small perturbations exhibits poor robustness.
wrong_explanation_1: Fairness concerns equitable outcomes across groups, not behavior under adversarial inputs.
wrong_explanation_2: Transparency concerns disclosing how the system works; it does not directly address adversarial robustness.
wrong_explanation_3: Privacy is about protecting personal data, not adversarial behavior.

scenario: A customer service chatbot built on Amazon Bedrock occasionally produces offensive or harmful responses. The team wants AWS-provided guardrails to filter inputs and outputs against configurable policies — without writing custom filtering code. Which Bedrock feature should they use?
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces configurable content policies on user inputs and model outputs — including denied topics, harmful content categories, profanity, sensitive information, and contextual grounding checks — without custom code.
wrong_explanation_1: Knowledge Bases provide retrieval grounding; they do not enforce harmful-content policies.
wrong_explanation_2: Agents orchestrate tasks; they do not filter content.
wrong_explanation_3: Model evaluation compares model quality; it does not act as a runtime filter.

scenario: Which responsible AI practice involves having humans review and correct model outputs in the loop, especially for high-stakes decisions?
correct_explanation: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) review embeds humans into the model's decision flow to validate, correct, or override outputs — especially important for high-stakes use cases. Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) is the AWS service that supports HITL workflows.
wrong_explanation_1: Quantization is a model-compression technique unrelated to oversight.
wrong_explanation_2: Hyperparameter sweeping is a training-time optimization, not an oversight practice.
wrong_explanation_3: Negative prompting suppresses unwanted content in image generation; it is not the same as human review.

scenario: An ML team needs to present a structured document describing a model's intended use, training data, performance, limitations, and risks for governance review. Which Amazon SageMaker feature is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: SageMaker Model Cards capture critical model documentation — intended use, training data, evaluation metrics, ethical considerations, risks, and limitations — in a structured format suited for governance and compliance reviews.
wrong_explanation_1: Model Dashboard provides operational status of running models; it is not the structured governance document the scenario describes.
wrong_explanation_2: JumpStart is the model hub for browsing and deploying models, not a governance document.
wrong_explanation_3: Studio Lab is a free Jupyter notebook environment, not a documentation feature.

scenario: AWS publishes AI Service Cards for many of its AI offerings (Rekognition, Textract, Transcribe, etc.). What is the primary purpose of these AI Service Cards?
correct_answer: To document the intended use cases, fairness considerations, and limitations of each AWS AI service for transparency
wrong_answer_1: To provide marketing brochures about the services
wrong_answer_2: To replace the AWS Acceptable Use Policy
correct_explanation: AWS AI Service Cards provide structured transparency about an AWS AI service — its intended use cases, fairness considerations, design choices, and limitations. They help customers make informed, responsible-use decisions.
wrong_explanation_1: AI Service Cards are formal, structured transparency documents — not marketing.
wrong_explanation_2: They do not replace the AUP, which governs acceptable use.
wrong_explanation_3: They are documentation, not IAM policies.

scenario: Which statement BEST captures the difference between MODEL INTERPRETABILITY and MODEL EXPLAINABILITY?
correct_answer: Interpretability is how directly a human can understand the model itself; explainability is the ability to describe why a model produced a specific output, often via post-hoc methods
wrong_answer_1: Interpretability and explainability mean exactly the same thing
wrong_answer_2: Interpretability refers only to deep neural networks
wrong_answer_3: Explainability is only relevant during data preparation
correct_explanation: Interpretability refers to how directly understandable the model's mechanism is (e.g., a small decision tree is highly interpretable). Explainability is the broader concept of describing why a model produced a specific output, often using techniques like SHAP for complex models.
wrong_explanation_1: While related, the terms have distinct, complementary meanings.
wrong_explanation_2: Interpretability applies to many model types; some (linear models, small trees) are inherently more interpretable than DNNs.
wrong_explanation_3: Explainability is relevant throughout the lifecycle, especially at inference time.

scenario: A regulator requires that an ML model's predictions be highly interpretable so the bank can clearly explain WHY each loan was approved or denied. Which model type provides the HIGHEST interpretability?
correct_explanation: Linear/logistic regression models are highly interpretable — coefficients directly indicate each feature's contribution to the prediction. This makes them the canonical choice when explaining individual decisions is critical.
wrong_explanation_1: Deep neural networks are highly capable but have low inherent interpretability; explanations require post-hoc techniques.
wrong_explanation_2: Random forests are ensembles of trees, more interpretable than DNNs but less than linear models.
wrong_explanation_3: LLMs have billions of parameters and are very difficult to interpret directly.

scenario: A team running ML workloads on Amazon SageMaker wants to control which users can launch training jobs, deploy endpoints, and access specific S3 buckets containing training data. Which AWS service should they use?
correct_explanation: IAM is the AWS service for defining who (users, roles) can do what (actions) on which resources. SageMaker permissions, S3 bucket access, and execution-role definitions all flow through IAM policies.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudWatch is for monitoring metrics and logs, not permission control.
wrong_explanation_2: KMS handles encryption keys; access decisions for SageMaker actions go through IAM.
wrong_explanation_3: GuardDuty is threat detection, not access control.

scenario: A regulated company wants to invoke Amazon Bedrock APIs from a VPC WITHOUT traffic traversing the public internet. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this private connectivity?
correct_explanation: AWS PrivateLink enables VPC endpoints to AWS services so that traffic remains on the AWS network and never traverses the public internet. Bedrock supports VPC endpoints via PrivateLink, addressing the requirement directly.
wrong_explanation_1: Direct Connect provides private connectivity between on-premises and AWS but does not by itself replace public service endpoints with private endpoints for VPC-to-Bedrock calls.
wrong_explanation_2: WAF protects web applications from common attacks; it does not establish private endpoint connectivity.
wrong_explanation_3: Route 53 Resolver handles DNS resolution between VPCs and on-premises; it is not the private endpoint mechanism for AWS services.

scenario: A team needs to encrypt the data their SageMaker training jobs read and write to S3 using a key the team can manage, rotate, and audit. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS KMS centrally creates, manages, rotates, and audits cryptographic keys used to encrypt data across AWS services including S3, EBS, and SageMaker resources. Customers can define key policies and audit usage via CloudTrail.
wrong_explanation_1: Macie discovers and protects sensitive data in S3 but does not manage cryptographic keys.
wrong_explanation_2: WAF protects web applications; it is not a key management service.
wrong_explanation_3: CloudWatch Logs collects logs; it does not manage encryption keys.

scenario: A health-care provider must keep patient training data inside the country in which the patient resides. Which data governance concept does this requirement BEST illustrate?
correct_explanation: Data residency is the requirement that data physically resides (and is processed) in a specific geographic area, typically driven by regulations. Selecting AWS Regions or using AWS Outposts/Local Zones can address residency requirements.
wrong_explanation_1: Data lineage tracks data flow and transformations end-to-end; it does not by itself dictate physical location.
wrong_explanation_2: Data labeling assigns ground truth to training examples; it is unrelated to geographic location.
wrong_explanation_3: Data wrangling cleans and transforms data; it is unrelated to residency.

scenario: A security team needs an audit log of every Bedrock InvokeModel API call made in their account — who called it, when, and from where — for compliance investigations. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this audit logging?
correct_explanation: AWS CloudTrail records every AWS API call in an account, including identity, source IP, time, and parameters. Bedrock API calls are recorded by CloudTrail, providing the audit trail compliance teams need.
wrong_explanation_1: CloudWatch metrics show numerical telemetry over time, not per-call audit history.
wrong_explanation_2: Trusted Advisor offers best-practice recommendations, not API call audit logs.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes; it is not the per-API call audit log service.

scenario: A company building an AI application on AWS needs to obtain AWS's SOC, ISO, and PCI compliance reports to share with their auditors. Which AWS service provides on-demand access to these compliance documents?
correct_explanation: AWS Artifact is the on-demand portal for AWS's own compliance reports and certifications — SOC, ISO, PCI-DSS, HIPAA-eligible services list, and similar documents. Auditors download AWS's compliance evidence from Artifact.
wrong_explanation_1: Audit Manager helps customers audit THEIR own AWS usage against frameworks. It does not provide AWS's own SOC/ISO reports — those come from Artifact.
wrong_explanation_2: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities, not compliance documentation.
wrong_explanation_3: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes; it is not the compliance-document distribution service.

scenario: A compliance officer wants to CONTINUOUSLY assess their AWS environment — including generative AI usage on Bedrock — against frameworks such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST, and a prebuilt framework for generative AI on AWS. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?
correct_explanation: AWS Audit Manager continuously collects evidence from the customer's AWS environment and maps it to controls in frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, NIST) including a prebuilt framework for generative AI on AWS. It produces audit-ready evidence packs.
wrong_explanation_1: Artifact distributes AWS's own compliance reports but does not continuously audit a customer's own AWS usage against frameworks.
wrong_explanation_2: GuardDuty performs threat detection, not framework-driven compliance assessment.
wrong_explanation_3: Trusted Advisor offers best-practice recommendations and does not produce framework-mapped evidence.

scenario: Under regulations like the EU GDPR, an individual may request that their personal data be deleted from a company's systems, including data used to train ML models. Which data governance concept does this requirement illustrate?
correct_answer: Right to be forgotten / data subject rights
correct_explanation: The "right to be forgotten" (under GDPR's data subject rights) gives individuals the ability to request deletion of their personal data. Organizations must consider this in training-data pipelines and retention plans, especially when personal data is used to train models.
wrong_explanation_1: Data residency concerns the geographic location of data, not deletion-on-request.
wrong_explanation_2: Data labeling assigns ground-truth tags; it is unrelated to deletion rights.
wrong_explanation_3: Hyperparameter tuning is a training-time concern, not a regulatory data-subject right.

scenario: A company wants to ensure that user prompts and model outputs in its Bedrock-based chatbot do not leak personally identifiable information (PII) like Social Security numbers and credit card numbers. Which Bedrock feature provides PII filtering at runtime?
correct_answer: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with sensitive information filters
wrong_answer_2: Amazon Comprehend (entity recognition only, no Bedrock integration)
correct_explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails includes sensitive-information filters that detect and redact PII (such as SSNs and credit cards) from user inputs and model outputs at runtime — purpose-built for the scenario.
wrong_explanation_1: Macie discovers sensitive data at rest in S3; it does not filter Bedrock prompts at runtime.
wrong_explanation_2: Comprehend's PII detection can be used externally but is not the integrated Bedrock runtime safeguard described.
wrong_explanation_3: Glue DataBrew is a data-preparation service, not a runtime PII filter for chatbots.
